The cause is in `src/leaks.py`, line 8. The check serializes the transcript with `json.dumps` and then looks for each secret as a plain substring of that JSON text.

`json.dumps` escapes every backslash as `\\`. So a Windows path in the transcript, `C:\Users\dana`, is stored in the JSON text as `C:\\Users\\dana`. A secret written as `C:\Users\dana` never matches that text, so the check lets the transcript through. A POSIX path has no backslashes, so `/home/dana` survives serialization unchanged and gets caught.

I reproduced it by calling `leaks()` directly on a transcript whose command is `type C:\Users\dana\notes.txt`:

- Secret `C:\Users\dana` (single backslashes): not found, `[]`.
- Secret `C:\\Users\\dana` (double backslashes): found. This only works because the escaped form happens to match, not because the check understands paths.
- Secret `/home/dana` against a `/home/dana` command: found.

The existing tests in `tests/test_leaks.py` only cover the `/home/dana` form, so nothing catches this. The fix belongs in `src/`, which I left untouched as you asked. The likely direction is to compare against the raw strings of the actions, not their JSON encoding, or to also check each secret in its escaped form. A test with a Windows home path would cover it.
